name: Bagrationi
summary: The Georgian royal family joined different kroner from the Caucasus and continued to rule its successor kingdoms after the fragmentation of the 15th century.
origin: The Bagraationi consolidated their power in Tao- Klarjetti during the Middle Ages. Bagrat III gathered the kronor of Abkhazia and the Georgians in 1008. The courtesan tradition linked the family to the biblical king David, a genealogy that was part of his religious legitimization.
history: David IV and Tamar witnessed a stage of military expansion and cultural flowering. His successors faced the Mongolian invasions and Timur campaigns. Family disputes and the autonomy of the great lords favored the emergence of separate kingdoms in Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti.
legacy: The branches retained the name Bagrationi and negotiated between the Ottoman, Persian and Russian powers. Kartli and Kakheti reunited under Heraclio II in 1762. The Russian annexation of 1801 ended with this monarchy; the one of Imereti survived until 1810. His lineage continued in exile and in the nobility of the Russian Empire.

name: Hohenzollern
summary: Burgraves of Nuremberg, who received Brandenburg in 1415, added the duchy of Prussia in 1618 and made their domains the kingdom of Prussia, a great power of the 18th century.
origin: Frederick VI of Nuremberg, of the Franconian branch, received from the Emperor Segismundo the margraviate of Brandenburg and his electoral dignity (1415-1417). Another branch ruled the Teutonic Prussia: Albert secularized it in 1525 and made it duchyd under Polish sovereignty.
history: In 1618, the elector John Segismundo inherited Prussia. After the devastation of the Thirty Years' War, Frederick William, the Grand Elector, built a permanent army and gained full sovereignty over Prussia in 1657. His son Frederick was crowned king in Prussia in 1701.
legacy: Frederick William I organized the administration and the army, and Frederick II conquered Silesia and participated in the Polish partitions. In the 19th century the house led German unification: William I was proclaimed emperor in 1871.

name: Valois
summary: A Capetian branch that ruled France and whose alliances connect French royalty with Brittany, Foix and Navarre.
origin: Charles of Valois, son of Philip III, named the branch. His son Philip VI acceded to the French crown in 1328. The lines of Orleans, Angoulême, Burgundy and other derivations kept their own names that help to follow their evolution.
history: The house went through the Hundred Years’ War and the struggles between its branches. Joan of France married the Duke of Brittany; Magdalena of France was the mother of Francisco Febo and Catherine of Navarre. The branches of Orleans and Angoulême then gathered rights that connected France, Brittany and Italy.
legacy: The Valois line ended with Henry III in 1589. Henry of Bourbon, king of Navarre and descendant of Louis IX by the branch of Robert, Count of Clermont, then entered the French crown.

name: Ivrea-Burgundy
summary: The branch of the comital house of Burgundy, of Ancárida origin (house of Ivrea), which reigned in Castilla and León from Alfonso VII (1126) to Peter I (1369). Another branch of the same house ruled Burgundy County.
origin: Raymond de Burgundy, son of Count William I of Burgundy, married Urraca, daughter of Alfonso VI in 1090. His son Alfonso VII succeeded his mother in 1126 and began the so-called Burgundian dynasty of Castile.
history: Alfonso VII redistributed Castile and León among his children. Alfonso VIII won in the Navas de Tolosa (1212). Ferdinand III, son of Berenguela and Alfonso IX, finally gathered the two crowns in 1230 and conquered Córdoba and Sevilla. The Sage was succeeded by Alfonso X, Sancho IV, Ferdinand IV and Alfonso XI.
legacy: Peter I died in Montiel in 1369 at the hands of his stepbrother Henry, the son of Alfonso XI and founder of the house of Trastámara. In the county of Burgundy, the canton IV and his daughters Joan II and Blanca, of the branch of the Chalon Counts, brought the comital inheritance to the kings of France. The historiography calls the Spanish branch house of Burgundy or Ivrea.

name: Albret
summary: From a French south-west lordship to Navarre: the Albrets grew up through political service, marriages and inheritance.
origin: The name Albret comes from the house's inheritance in the south-west of France. Arnaud-Amanieu and his son Charles I expanded the family position by serving the French monarchy. The connection with the crown of the Navarre came several generations later.
history: Charles I died in Agincourt. His daughter Joan married John I of Foix, while the lordship continuity passed through Charles II and the descendants of John of Tartas to Alain. John III, son of Alain, married Catherine of Navarre. The conquest of 1512 profoundly altered the position of that couple, whose descendants retained the monarchy to the north of the Pyrenees.
legacy: Henry II and Joan III linked the house to the political and religious transformations of the 16th century. The marriage of Joan with Anthony de Bourbon was the origin of the Navarre position of his son Henry, future Henry IV of France. Charlotte of Albret offers another connection, with the Borja.

name: Paleólogo-Montferrat
summary: An inheritance transmitted from a Byzantine empress created an Italian branch of Palaiologoi.
origin: Theodore I was the son of Andronikos II and Irene de Montferrat. His mother's rights led him to the marquisate after the male extinction of the Aleramici.
history: The generations of John II and Teodoro II linked with Majorca; those of John James, William VIII and Boniface III intertwined with Savoy and Saluzzo. The family lived together with clashes over territories and feudal rights.
legacy: The death of John George in 1533 opened the inheritance. In 1536 the imperial resolution recognized the rights of Margaret Paleologue, wife of Frederick II Gonzaga, and the marquisate passed to his descendants.

name: Árpád
summary: The Hungarian national dynasty. He descended from Árpád, the leader of the Magiar conquest, and reigned in Hungary from the coronation of Stephen I to the death of Andrew III in 1301.
origin: Arpád directed the Magiars in the occupation of the Carpathian basin at the end of the 9th century. His descendant Stephen I received the royal crown with the approval of Pope Silvestre II and organized the kingdom according to the frank model.
history: The Arpád joined Croatia to the Hungarian crown in the early 12th century. Andrew II granted the nobility the Golden Bullet (1222), and his son Bela IV reconstructed the kingdom after the Mongol invasion of 1241-1242. The house was related to the great European dynasties: Violant, daughter of Andrew II, was queen of Aragon as wife of James I.
legacy: Andrew III, the last male of the dynasty, died in 1301. The papacy then backed Charles Robert of Anjou, a descendant of the Árpád by female line, who reigned from 1308. The crown of St Stephen remained the symbol of the legitimacy of the kingdom.

name: Zrinski
summary: From Croatian patrimony to the Ottoman border and to the trilvane links.
origin: The Zrinski came from the Šubić of Bribir and took their name from the Zrin domain in the 14th century.
history: The descendants of Nikola IV passes through Juraj IV and Juraj V to the brothers Nikola VII and Petar IV. His governments as bans lived with the authority of the king of Croatia. Marriages with the Frankopan reinforced a network of domains and relationships that reached the coast.
legacy: Petar's execution in 1671 broke his political position. His daughter Jelena, wife of Francis I Rákóczi, extended the family's ties with Hungary and Transylvania. His son Francis II led the rebellion against the Habsburgs of the early 18th century.

name: Hetúmida
summary: The Hetumidas ruled the Cilician Armenia and linked the Mediterranean to the Crusades with the powers of the Asian interior.
origin: The family of the Hetumidas acquired the crown by the marriage of Hetum I with Elizabeth, the heir of Leon the Magnificent, in 1226. The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia had its capital in Sis and controlled steps, fortresses and ports of the Eastern Mediterranean.
history: The kings sought alliances with the crossed states and the Mongols to hold their position in front of the neighbouring powers. The marriages with other ruling families expanded their connections: Rita of Armenia married the Byzantine co-emperor Michael IX Paleologist.
legacy: Mamluk campaigns weakened the resources of the kingdom and Mongolian military cooperation proved irregular. At the same time, the courts and monasteries promoted enlightened manuscripts and a culture that combined Armenian, Byzantine and Latino traditions. The passage from the crown to the Lusignan in the 14th century extended that network of relationships before the fall of Sis in 1375.

name: Welf
summary: The Welf moved from the great duchies of Saxony and Bavaria to a network of principalities of Brunswick- Lüneburg.
origin: The youngest house of the Welf was born from the marriage of Azzo II of East with Cunegunda of Altdorf. Their descendants gathered the duchies of Bavaria and Saxony. Henry the Lion extended his power in the German north and favored the development of Brunswick and Lübeck.
history: Henry's conflict with Frederick Barbarossa culminated in the loss of his duchies in 1180. His son, Otto IV, became emperor, while another grandson, Otto the Child, received in 1235 the new Brunswick- Lüneburg duchy, built on family inheritance.
legacy: The successive partitions originated principalities such as Wolfenbüttel, Grubenhagen, Göttingen and Calenberg. Each line retained dynastic rights and was able to inherit the estates of another upon its extinction. The branch of Calenberg, later known as Hanover, obtained electoral dignity and reached the British crown in 1714.

name: Lorraine
summary: The ducal house of Lorraine maintained a border inheritance between France and the Empire and extended into Guise and the Habsburgs.
origin: Gerardo de Alsace received the Alta Lorraine in 1048. His descendants ruled the duchy for centuries. The death of Charles II in 1431 transmitted the rights of his branch to his daughter Elizabeth and her husband, René de Anjou.
history: The inheritance later passed to the Vaudémont line. René II defeated Charles the Bold before Nancy in 1477 and assured the duchy. The descendants of their son Claudio formed the House of Guise in France, while the main line was facing the growing pressure of the French monarchy.
legacy: The wars of the 17th century caused ducal occupations and exiles. Francisco Stephen resigned Lorraine in the negotiations that accompanied his marriage to Maria Teresa de Habsburg. He received Tuscany and his descendants founded the Habsburgo-Lorraine house. The duchy was left in the hands of Estanislao Leszczyński and joined France after his death in 1766.

name: Grailly

origin: The Grailly belonged to the nobility networks that connected the Savoyard sphere to the French southwest. Archambaud's marriage to Isabel de Foix- Castellbó linked the family to the counties and the Pyrenian viscounties.
history: Elizabeth succeeded her brother Mateo in 1398. Archambaud participated in the government through his marriage, while the hereditary right came from her. His son John I continued the line known as Foix-Grailly and connected him to the Albret by marriage to Joan de Albret.
legacy: Isabel passed on the property of Foix to her children with Archambaud. The new line, known as Foix-Grailly, retained the name and rights of the mother's house and extended its links to the crown of Navarre.

name: Farnesio
summary: The Farnese passed from the nobility of Lazio to the papacy and a duchy who linked their interests to the Hispanic monarchy.
origin: The family accumulated military lordships and services in the territory of Viterbo. Alexander Farnese developed his ecclesiastical career until he was elected Pope as Paul III in 1534. In 1545 he created the duchy of Parma and Piacenza for his son Peter Louis.
history: The murder of Peter Louis in 1547 opened a crisis that his son Ottavio resolved by agreement with the papacy and the Habsburgs. Ottavio married Margaret of Austria. His son Alexander served Philip II and led the armies of the monarchy in the Netherlands.
legacy: The dukes sponsored buildings, artists and collections that gave Parma and Rome prestige. Ranuccio I consolidated ducal administration. Anthony's death in 1731 ended with the male ruling line. Elisabeth Farnese, queen of Spain, defended his son Charles's rights to the Italian inheritance and transmitted the great family collections to his descendants.

name: Piccolomini
summary: The goods, bankers and Sienese owners were distributed in several branches and reached the papacy with Pius II and Pius III.
origin: Documented in Siena during the Middle Ages, the family developed commercial and financial activities before consolidating a wide territorial inheritance. Its different branches retained links and a shared identity.
history: Aneas Silvio Piccolomini was chosen Pius II in 1458 and favored the position of his relatives. His sister Laudomia married Nanni Todeschini: the children of this union adopted the mother's name when their uncle was raised to the pontificate. One of them, Francesco, became Pope Pius III in 1503.
legacy: The adoption of the surname by the children of Laudomia extended the name Piccolomini through the mother's descendants. Other branches maintained their own alliances. The family history links the humanism of Pius II, the curial power and the inheritance strategies of the Sienese nobility.
